body:
Speech to text (STT) accuracy depends on three things: the quality of your audio, how people speak, and the words they use. Noise and heavy compression strip detail from a recording, with even strong models struggling with overlapping voices or unfamiliar jargon. This guide shows where each STT problem comes from and how to fix it.

Transcription errors rarely stay in the transcript. A misheard drug name in a clinical note or a wrong account number in a call log carries into every system that uses that text, from search and analytics to AI agents that act on what was said. Poor accuracy also adds review time, because someone has to find and correct the mistakes by hand.

The good news is that most STT accuracy problems are fixable. Many of these fixes only require slight changes to your existing configurations or recording setups, which means you can fix your problem without having to change your model settings.

You may also see this topic called speech recognition accuracy, ASR accuracy, or transcription accuracy. Speech to text, speech recognition, and automatic speech recognition (ASR) all describe the same process of converting spoken audio into written text. The fixes in this guide apply whichever term you use.

## Summary

• Speech to text accuracy depends on audio input quality, speaker dynamics, and lexical and contextual issues.

• To fix an accuracy problem, find where in the pipeline (input, processing, or output) you can make a change.

• Record at 16 kHz or higher, use lossless formats, and place microphones four to six inches from the speaker.

• Use voice isolation, diarization or multichannel recording, and keyterm prompting to handle noise, overlapping speakers, and specialized vocabulary.

• Measure accuracy with word error rate (WER), and check which errors matter most for your use case.

## What causes speech to text accuracy problems?

Imagine someone asks you to transcribe an audio recording of a thickly accented professor describing complex theoretical physics, recorded in a crowded restaurant with background music and ambient chatter. Digital computer systems aren't natively attuned to acoustic variability. It takes significant training and fine-tuning to make STT work effectively , and while modern AI tooling is very effective, many issues can still impact output. But by understanding what they are, you can address them in your transcription workflows.

There are three main causes for inaccurate speech to text conversion:

• Issues with audio input quality

• Lexical and contextual issues

Each cause needs a different fix, which the sections below cover in turn.

## Audio quality issues

First, the audio recording itself can have issues. Microphone issues could lead to speech becoming distorted or clipped. Reverb due to the acoustics of the venue, a poor signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) on the recording, or a low sampling rate on the recording could all potentially strip away important phonetic information from recordings.

## Speaker dynamics

A single speaker with a neutral accent, speaking in a quiet venue, will be relatively easy to transcribe. But that’s rarely the type of recording we want transcribed. Unfamiliar accents and choppy or simply non-traditional speaking cadence can throw off an STT model trained on standardized speech. Cross-talk or overlapping speakers can also disrupt a model’s ability to accurately parse what’s being said.

## Lexical and contextual issues

Lastly, speech content can also challenge some STT models. Industry jargon and new product names might not be language an STT model has encountered in training. As it selects the most statistically likely output, speech that’s unfamiliar may not be a top prediction. Numerical or mathematical expressions, or speech that might otherwise be written numerically, also might not transcribe clearly.

Homophones are words that sound the same but are spelled differently. An STT model needs enough contextual understanding to distinguish between them. For example, “the bear ambled across the bare mountainside.” The model would need to know the animal is spelled “bear” and the adjective for an uncovered surface is spelled “bare.”

## How to fix speech to text accuracy problems from audio to output

Speech to text processing occurs in a series of well-defined steps. To fix an accuracy issue, you need to identify where in that pipeline you can make a change. Broadly speaking, the STT process breaks down into:

Each stage has its own failure modes and its own fixes.

## Upstream input accuracy issues

There could be issues with the environment in which you’re recording. Common issues here include background noise or echoes. The recording equipment could also be the source of an issue if it’s faulty.

Fixing issues in this stage typically involves isolating what is causing the problem and resolving it. For example, if you know that the STT tool struggles with loud backgrounds, then hosting conversations in an environment that you have more control over is a good idea.

For any noise you can’t avoid, apply voice isolation before the audio reaches the model.

## Accuracy issues in processing

How you configure your API to an STT engine can affect processing. Prompt structure and the model you choose can also affect quality and the number of inaccuracies.

Fixing issues in this stage means testing your setup against your own audio. Run the same sample recordings through each candidate model, compare their word error rates , and then change one setting as a time to refine.

If a model keeps missing one type of speech, such as a noisy call or a certain regional accent, test out different models for their accuracy in the exact environment you’ll be using.

## Downstream output accuracy issues

This is your quality-control layer, where specialized processes clean up transcription errors and ambiguities your primary engine might have missed. STT pipelines regularly use rule-based pattern matching to standardize form
